ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory enhanced CDD before registration and before admitting any partner: (i) run PEP screening for all general partners, limited partners and UBOs against domestic and foreign PEP lists; (ii) screen against UN Sanctions List and Canadian sanctions regulations under the United Nations Act and Special Economic Measures Act; and (iii) run OFAC SDN screening as part of the bank/clearing risk review. FINTRAC records must be kept for five years after the end of the business relationship; ultimate beneficial ownership is identified at 25% or more using a risk-based approach.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Ontario Business Registry (OBR) - Companies and Personal Property search portal operated by the Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery; https://www.ontario.ca/page/ontario-business-registry
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: The LP name must be in English or French, or in either language with an equivalent version, and must be written in Roman/Latin script. Non-English/non-French names must be transliterated into Latin characters. The name must include a prescribed limited-partnership designation: 'Limited Partnership', 'L.P.'/'LP', or French 'société en commandite'/'S.E.C.'.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If the Ontario Business Registry refuses a name because it is confusingly similar to an existing name, prepare a written Request for Name Review to the Director, Companies and Personal Property Branch, Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery, within 30 days of refusal. Attach the NUANS search report, the refusal notice, a revised proposed name, and submissions distinguishing the goods/services; obtain written consent from the prior name holder or file a waiver/undertaking if applicable. The Director's written determination may be challenged by judicial review to the Divisional Court of Ontario.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permitted as a registered-office address only if the service provider maintains a physical Ontario street address and accepts service of process; a P.O. Box is not a valid registered office. For this Asian supermarket/grocery business, the operational location must be a real leased or owned retail premise with municipal zoning, health and food-safety approval; a virtual office cannot supply commercial substance for day-to-day grocery retailing.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Registered office/books: <5% annual probability; AML/KYC files: 15-20% if selected for regulatory review; physical grocery premises: 60-80% annual likelihood of unannounced public-health/food-safety, weights-and-measures, fire-code or municipal business-licensing inspection under O. Reg. 493/17 (Ontario Food Premises Regulation).

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) — federal tax authority for GST/HST and Canadian income tax administration; Ontario Ministry of Finance and Ontario Business Registry — provincial tax and business registration. Portal: CRA My Business Account (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/cra-login-services.html); Ontario Business Registry (https://www.ontario.ca/page/ontario-business-registry).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: For a foreign-owned Ontario Limited Partnership, the operative statutory tax ID for GST/HST is the CRA Business Number (BN). Apply online through CRA My Business Account or by Form RC1 (Request for Business Number); CRA may require the Ontario Limited Partnerships Act registration to be completed first through the Ontario Business Registry. The application must identify the partnership, the general partner, and the limited partners. CRA will issue a 9-digit base BN plus a program-account suffix such as 123456789 RT0001, which must be displayed on invoices, included in HST returns, and stated on customs/export documentation. The CRA BN functions as the federal TIN and GST/HST registration number for the LP.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada has no U.S.-style check-the-box election. A Canadian limited partnership is fiscally transparent by statutory design and cannot elect to be taxed as a corporation for Canadian income tax purposes. Available elections include partnership rollover elections under the Income Tax Act (e.g., ITA s.97(2) for property contributed to a partnership and s.98(3) for transfers of partnership property to a corporation). Hybrid mismatch rules operate automatically by statute and are not elective; no domestic opt-out is available.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Harmonized Sales Tax (HST) — a value-added tax administered federally by CRA, comprising 5% federal GST and 8% Ontario provincial component; Ontario no longer imposes a separate retail sales tax.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: C$30,000 CAD. A person is a small supplier until worldwide taxable supplies exceed C$30,000 in a calendar quarter or over the immediately preceding four calendar quarters. Once the threshold is exceeded, GST/HST registration is mandatory. A physical retail grocery location in Ontario also creates continuing Canadian nexus; even below the threshold, the LP may voluntarily register to claim input tax credits.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No real-time fiscal clearance, mandatory digital stamping, or continuous transaction control e-invoicing regime applies in Canada for grocery retail. GST/HST registrants must issue invoices or receipts showing the supplier's BN and the HST charged. Electronic documents are acceptable; voluntary B2B e-invoicing may use the Pan-Canadian Peppol network. POS receipts issued through Interac or credit-card terminals satisfy the point-of-sale invoice obligation, but detailed invoices must be available to CRA on request.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Goods exported from Canada are zero-rated under ETA Schedule VI, Part V. The registrant must retain evidence that the goods were physically removed from Canada, normally by (a) the supplier exporting the goods itself, (b) the supplier shipping via a common carrier or freight forwarder for export, or (c) delivering the goods to a non-resident purchaser who exports them within a commercially reasonable time. Services supplied to non-residents may be zero-rated as offshore services unless they relate to Canadian real property, tangible personal property located in Canada at the time of supply, or services to an individual present in Canada. Export zero-rating allows full input tax credits for HST paid on purchases supporting the export. Basic groceries sold domestically may also be zero-rated, but export zero-rating specifically requires documented physical export.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (Canada Customs Form B13A or equivalent electronic custom-terms data/CUS-IFP for commercial exports)
Bill of Lading (ocean, air, or truck) showing movement from Canada to a foreign destination
Inward Remittance Certificate (bank or foreign-exchange record evidencing receipt of export proceeds from the non-resident buyer)
Commercial invoice and contract of sale showing the non-resident consignee and Incoterms
Packing list and carrier/freight-forwarder certificate of departure from Canada
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA treats export zero-rating as a high-risk review area. If the required export evidence is incomplete, inconsistent, or fraudulent, CRA may deny zero-rating, reassess HST at 13% in Ontario, disallow or claw back related input tax credits, charge arrears interest, and impose civil false-statement or gross-negligence penalties under the Excise Tax Act. Criminal prosecution is possible for intentional evasion. The ordinary CRA assessment period is four years, but it is extended indefinitely where misrepresentation, wilful default, or fraud is established.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada); prudential supervision of deposit-taking institutions by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI); cross-border transaction reporting and AML/ATF supervision by the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC); sanctions administration by Global Affairs Canada and enforcement by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar (CAD) is freely convertible on both current-account and capital-account transactions; Canada has accepted IMF Article VIII obligations and imposes no general exchange controls under the Currency Act, the Bank of Canada Act, or the Bank Act. Capital injections by non-resident limited partners, foreign-currency account maintenance, and repatriation of partnership distributions require no Bank of Canada or OSFI prior approval. Profit and capital remittances to non-resident partners are nevertheless subject to Part XIII withholding tax under the Income Tax Act (Canada) at the statutory rate of 25%, generally reduced to 15% or less under an applicable tax treaty (for example, the Canada-United States Convention), and to comprehensive OFSI-style sanctions screening. The proposed grocery-retail limited partnership will not trigger Investment Canada Act review given the WTO enterprise-value thresholds are unlikely to be exceeded.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. Canada maintains no statutory timeline, mandatory conversion ratio, or surrender mechanism for export proceeds. As a net importer of Asian condiments and vegetables, the LP is under no obligation to convert foreign-currency receipts into CAD. The entity may lawfully hold USD, CNY/CNH, JPY, HKD, EUR, and other foreign-currency operating accounts at Schedule I banks and may use intercompany or receivable proceeds to settle offshore supplier invoices without forced conversion. The only applicable statutory reporting duty is FINTRAC's large electronic fund transfer reporting for any wire or electronic transfer of CAD 10,000 or more in a single 24-hour period.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Ancillary feasibility only. Wise Payments Canada Inc., Airwallex (Canada) Limited, and similar entities are FINTRAC-registered money services businesses (MSBs), not Schedule I or Schedule II banks. They cannot provide Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC) insured operating accounts, Interac Direct Payment merchant clearing, credit-card acquiring settlement, or commercial documentary-credit issuance. Legally, operating a deposit-taking business without a Bank Act authorization is prohibited; accordingly, an Ontario-domiciled EMI/MSB relationship is viable solely as a supplementary disbursement rail for low-value supplier payments and efficient FX conversion (e.g., paying small Chinese or Southeast Asian vendors). The primary treasury architecture must be anchored at a chartered Canadian bank.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: FINTRAC's customer-identification rules permit non-face-to-face verification using reliable, independent sources, but individual banks retain discretion to require in-branch attendance. For an Ontario limited partnership whose general partner is a Canadian corporation with resident directors, remote video onboarding is generally accepted by the major banks. The Ontario-registered attorney for service and the corporate general partner's authorized signatories must provide a notarized incumbency certificate, certificate of corporate status, and board resolutions authorizing account opening. Non-resident limited partners are not required to appear in person; however, if the general partner is itself foreign or a non-resident individual is designated as an authorized signatory, banks will typically impose an enhanced due diligence protocol, including an in-branch interview at an Ontario commercial banking centre, extended beneficial-ownership disclosure, and independent verification of the foreign entity's existence and good standing before any transaction is permitted.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident limited partners holding more than 25% economic interest without transparent source of funds, triggering enhanced due diligence under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Notarized limited partnership agreement and all amending declarations; Certificate of Limited Partnership (Ontario Form 3) from the Ontario Business Registry; certified register of limited partners with full legal name, residential address, citizenship, capital contribution schedule, and percentage interest; bank reference letters and three months of originating-bank account statements for each non-resident partner; notarized Source of Wealth and Source of Funds reports prepared by a licensed CPA or law firm; counsel opinion confirming the private placement exemption under National Instrument 45-106; sanctions screening results against FINTRAC, Global Affairs Canada, UN, EU, and OFAC lists.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cash-intensive fresh-vegetable and condiment retail sales generating daily cash deposits disproportionate to declared store volumes, raising structuring suspicions.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified point-of-sale audit trail from Interac Direct Payment and credit-card acquiring terminals; daily cash-count sheets reconciled to electronic journal tapes; perpetual inventory records with purchase invoices for imported product; CRA HST/GST returns and business-number registration; written cash-management and deposit policy approved by the general partner; monthly store-level income statement and bank-deposit reconciliation prepared by an independent CPA.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Repeated cross-border wire disbursements to Asian trading counterparties in jurisdictions perceived as high-risk without adequate trade documentation.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Complete import documentary package per shipment: commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading or airway bill, Canadian customs entry (CBSA Form B3-3), and customs release; supplier onboarding file containing beneficial-ownership attestation, business-licence copies, sanctions screening, and AML questionnaire; historical invoices and payment tenors evidencing a consistent commercial pattern; freight-forwarder and customs-broker statements; documented FX hedging policy explaining the economic purpose of each outward payment.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Discrepancy between the registered office address used for LP registration and the physical supermarket premises, or use of a corporate service provider as registered attorney, raising shell-structure concerns.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Ontario Business Registry extracts confirming registered office and attorney for service; commercial lease agreement for the physical grocery store in Ontario; municipal business licence and Provincial food-premises/public-health inspection certificates; general partner's articles of incorporation, certificate of corporate status, and signatory resolution; written explanation of the registered-office/service-agent arrangement with any third-party agent agreement provided.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Mismatch between legal entity names on banking instructions, supplier contracts, and customs documentation, creating identity-verification failures.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Convenience letter signed by the general partner confirming all account and trade names; certified true copies of the limited partnership declaration and general partner's incorporating documents; store licences and brand registration if a trade name is used; notarized specimen signatures of all authorized signatories; completed FINTRAC identity-verification forms supported by passport, driver's licence, or equivalent government-issued identification for every signatory.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Non-resident limited-partner capital contributions must be remitted by SWIFT MT103 from the partner's home-country bank directly into the LP's CAD Capital Escrow Account at a Canadian Schedule I bank. The wire instruction must carry the LP's full registered legal name, the account number, the receiver bank's SWIFT/BIC, and the remittance narrative: 'CA_LP - CAPITAL CONTRIBUTION - [partner legal name]'. No exchange-control approval is required for CAD, USD, CNY/CNH, JPY, HKD, or EUR. Where the contribution is denominated in a foreign currency, the Canadian bank will convert at a spot rate quoted under its standard FX terms, and the economic terms must be documented in a confirmation ticket. Each electronic transfer of CAD 10,000 or more is reported by the bank to FINTRAC, and the originator must provide source-of-funds evidence on request. Escrow release conditions should include receipt of the wire, issuance of a partnership capital-account credit memorandum, updating of the LP's capital ledger, and a legal opinion confirming valid Ontario registration and the general partner's authority to open the account and accept capital.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Supplier payments for imported Asian condiments and vegetables clear through four primary rails: (a) SWIFT MT103/MT202 direct high-value wire settlements to Asian beneficiary banks (e.g., HSBC Hong Kong, DBS Singapore, Standard Chartered Shanghai); (b) commercial letters of credit issued by the Canadian bank via SWIFT MT700 to the supplier's confirming bank, with settlement on presentation of compliant transport, invoice, and inspection documents (MT754/MT756 followed by MT202); (c) documentary collections (documents against payment or acceptance) for established suppliers to reduce letter-of-credit costs; and (d) cross-border CAD/USD ACH using the Canadian account's US routing-number service for high-frequency, low-value payments to US-based wholesalers. For Chinese suppliers, the bank may route through cross-border RMB (CNH) clearing via CIPS or an offshore CNH account, subject to applicable Canadian economic sanctions, Global Affairs Canada export/import permits, and CBSA customs documentation. All outward disbursements must be supported by a purchase order, commercial invoice, customs entry, and, where applicable, an executed FX hedge ticket documenting the rate-lock.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable outright FX forwards (spot-deferred forwards) on CAD/USD, CAD/CNH, CAD/JPY, CAD/EUR, CAD/AUD, and CAD/HKD for tenors of up to 24 months, executed under an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement with the Canadian Schedule I bank.

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) on restricted or less-liquid Asian currencies (INR, KRW, VND, TWD, THB, PHP, IDR) on standard ISDA/NDF documentation, cash-settled in CAD or USD, permissible where the underlying is a committed import trade payable.

Cross-currency swaps (fixed-floating CCS) on CAD/USD, CAD/CNH, and CAD/JPY to hedge longer-dated supply-chain payables and to convert non-resident partner capital contributions into working capital without rolling short-term forwards.
Vanilla European FX options (call/put spreads or outright puts) on CAD/USD and CAD/CNH to protect minimum/maximum procurement conversion rates while retaining upside on favorable moves.

Natural hedging through multi-currency operating accounts (USD, CNH/CNY, JPY, HKD, EUR) that permit settlement of offshore supplier invoices directly from cash collections attributed to the same currencies, reducing the notional of external derivatives.
FX swap/tom-next roll structures permitted as liquidity-management instruments to manage day-to-day funding gaps between CAD operating accounts and foreign-currency disbursement accounts.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Ontario Limited Partnership Annual Return (Form 3 under section 10(1) of the Limited Partnerships Act)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery / Ontario Business Registry (ServiceOntario)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after the end of the limited partnership's fiscal year; the obligation recurs annually on each fiscal year-end anniversary.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to file is an offence under section 10(2) of the Limited Partnerships Act; on conviction the limited partnership is liable to a fine of not more than C$2,000. Continued default for two or more consecutive years may result in administrative strike-off of the LP registration from the Ontario register.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No statutory audit threshold is imposed by the Limited Partnerships Act (Ontario) on a limited partnership. An independent audit becomes legally mandatory only if the LP is a reporting issuer under the Securities Act (Ontario), if securities legislation requires audited financial statements, or if the limited partnership agreement expressly imposes an audit obligation. Lender or investor requirements are contractual and do not constitute statutory audit triggers.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: For a private Ontario limited partnership, financial statements may be prepared in accordance with Canadian Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE) under the CPA Canada Handbook. IFRS is mandatory if the LP is a reporting issuer or otherwise falls within Part I of the Handbook. For income tax purposes, the Income Tax Act (Canada) applies generally accepted accounting principles, subject to specific statutory adjustments. Full books and source records must be maintained; CRA requires at least six years of retention, and this matrix applies a seven-year retention standard.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Ontario does not require a separate annual UBO confirmation filing for a limited partnership. The public LP declaration discloses only the general partners and registered office; limited partners are not part of the public register. The LP must maintain an internal register that accurately reflects all partners, capital contributions, withdrawals, and allocations, and must update that register upon any transfer of partnership interests. If the general partner is a CBCA or ONCA corporation, that corporation must maintain an individuals with significant control (ISC) register and comply with applicable corporate changes reporting; no LP-specific UBO attestation is filed with the Ontario Business Registry.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Partners (general and limited partners, showing capital contributions, withdrawals, and profit/loss allocations)
Minute Book / Resolution Record of the General Partner
Books and Records of Account (including receipts, ledger, vouchers, bank statements, and source documents)

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 75 - 250 per annum (approximately CAD 100 - 350), depending on agent services and inclusion of a physical registered office address in Ontario.
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 2,500 - 7,500 for a review engagement; USD 10,000 - 25,000 for a full independent audit of a single-location specialty grocery limited partnership.

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: LP is a pass-through entity; no corporate income tax at entity level. Partners are taxed individually. No statutory tax holidays apply. Small business deduction may be available to corporate partners if eligible.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T5013 (Partnership Information Return) filed via CRA My Business Account or authorized tax software
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Due within 5 months after the partnership's fiscal year-end

field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Provide full legal name and CRA business number; non-resident partners must be identified with their country of residence.
Enter the fiscal year-end in YYYY-MM-DD format; ensure consistency with financial statements.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Allocation of income or loss to each partner
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Allocate income based on partnership agreement; non-resident partners must receive a T5013 slip and may be subject to Part XIII withholding on their share.
Report gross revenue and deductible expenses; non-resident partners must ensure expenses are allocated in accordance with Canadian tax rules.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty of $100 per day, up to $2,500, plus additional penalties for failure to provide information slips. Interest may also accrue on unpaid amounts.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% (applies to non-resident partners on allocated income, not dividends; partnership distributions are not dividends)
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To claim treaty relief, non-resident partners must provide a Certificate of Residency (Form NR116) or a Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) from their home jurisdiction. The partnership must withhold at the reduced treaty rate if the certificate is provided before the payment or allocation.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Royalties: statutory rate 25%, reduced to 15% under many DTAs. Interest: statutory rate 25%, but often exempt for arm's length interest under treaties.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: CAD 1,000,000 gross revenue threshold for the taxpayer and all non-resident related parties
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not have specific Economic Substance Regulations (ESR), but the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR) applies to transactions lacking economic substance. The partnership must have genuine business purpose and commercial substance.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Willful omission of income, false deductions, or deliberate misrepresentation of financial records to reduce tax liability
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Criminal prosecution under the Income Tax Act; fines up to 200% of the tax evaded, imprisonment up to 5 years, and civil penalties
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally liable for unpaid corporate taxes and penalties if they participated in or acquiesced to the evasion; travel bans and asset freezes may be imposed.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating as a pass-through entity without real business operations, employees, or physical presence, solely to obtain tax benefits
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: GAAR reassessment, denial of tax benefits, and penalties up to 50% of the tax benefit; potential criminal charges for fraud
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally liable for taxes and penalties if they knowingly participated in the sham; possible injunctions and dissolution orders.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failure to implement anti-money laundering controls, report suspicious transactions, or verify customer identity under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Administrative monetary penalties up to CAD 1,000,000 for individuals and CAD 2,000,000 for entities; criminal penalties including imprisonment
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally liable for penalties if they failed to establish adequate compliance programs; travel bans and asset seizures may occur.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Setting intercompany prices for goods, services, or intangibles that deviate from arm's length, resulting in profit shifting to low-tax jurisdictions
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Adjustment of taxable income, penalties up to 10% of the understated tax, and interest on unpaid amounts; potential double taxation
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally liable for penalties if they knowingly approved non-arm's length pricing; travel bans and criminal prosecution for tax evasion may apply.
